phonemes.desc: Short epsilon [e], the prepositional prefix ἐπί- opening the name.
Plain pi [p], unaspirated as in Greek spelling before another consonant.
Long eta [ɛː] with acute pitch — the stressed peak of the name.
Aspirated theta [tʰ], the same root that gives Promētheus his "forethought".
Long upsilon with acute, the agent-noun ending: "the one who thinks".

pronunciation.approximation: 'eh-pee-MAY-thay-oos' — stress falls on the long middle syllable; the final syllable is held and ends with an -oos sound.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἐπιμηθεύς (Epimētheús), the brother of Promētheus in Hesiod

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Epimetheus, the form preserved in Roman mythography

pronunciation.note: Epimētheus is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἐπιμηθεύς carries both stress (acute on the long ē) and length (ē, ús), distinctive features the ASCII form flattens.

domains.title: The Afterthinker
domains.subtitle: Hindsight, Rash Acceptance, and the Release of Evils
domains.lead: Epimētheus is the twin brother of Promētheus, but where his brother thinks ahead, Epimētheus thinks behind. In Hesiod he is the one who accepts Pandora — the all-gifted woman — and with her the jar that releases sorrow, toil, and disease into the human world. His name is not a flaw in Greek; it is a role: the necessary complement to foresight, the moment after the choice when consequence becomes visible.

cards.name: The Jar of Evils
cards.desc: Hesiod says Epimētheus lifted the lid on the great jar and scattered evils among mortals; only Elpis, Hope, remained inside.

cards.name: Pandora
cards.desc: The "all-gifted" woman fashioned by the gods and sent to Epimētheus as a punishment for Promētheus's theft of fire.

cards.name: Brother of Forethought
cards.desc: Promētheus warns him not to accept gifts from Zeús; Epimētheus forgets the warning and acts on impulse.

cards.name: Aftermath
cards.desc: His myth turns on the moment after: the recognition that some gifts are also judgments, and that hindsight arrives too late.

symbols.name: The storage-jar (pithos)
symbols.meaning: The vessel from which every human ill escaped, and in which Hope alone remained

symbols.name: Pandora
symbols.meaning: The crafted gift he accepted, embodying both allure and consequence

symbols.name: Brother pair
symbols.meaning: Forethought and afterthought as two sides of mortal decision

symbols.name: Ember or fading flame
symbols.meaning: The aftermath of Promētheus's fire — the heat that remains when the moment of choice has passed

mythology.lead: Epimētheus appears most fully in Hesiod's didactic poems, where he is less a hero than a caution: the type of mortal who acts first and understands later.

myths.title: The Titan Brothers
myths.text: Epimētheus and Promētheus are sons of the Titan Iapetos and the Oceanid Klymenē. While Promētheus shapes humanity from clay and steals fire for mortals, Epimētheus distributes qualities among the animals and leaves human beings naked and unprotected — a double act of unequal cunning.

myths.title: The Gift of Pandora
myths.text: After Promētheus deceives Zeús at Mekonē, the king of the gods fashions Pandora as a "beautiful evil" and sends her with a jar to Epimētheus. Promētheus has warned his brother never to accept a gift from Olympian Zeús, but Epimētheus takes her in. Before he can think of the warning, he has lifted the lid, and countless sorrows fly out among humankind. Only Elpis — Hope — is caught under the rim and remains with mortals.

myths.title: The Hindsight God
myths.text: Later poets and philosophers make Epimētheus a figure for the wisdom that comes too late. Plato names him in the Protagoras as the one who, lacking foresight, left humans without natural defenses — a fault that Promētheus tried to repair with fire and the arts. In every version his role is the same: he is the god of the second thought, the one who understands only after the damage is done.

lore.syncretism: Epimētheus has no Roman cult or foreign double; his afterlife is philosophical and literary. The Platonic Protagoras retells the distribution of qualities as a lesson in human lack and compensation. Renaissance and Enlightenment writers used him as an emblem of impulsive judgment, and modern risk-theory sometimes borrows his name for the habit of acting before the consequences are understood. His closest mythic kin is his own brother: Promētheus is the crime, Epimētheus is the regret.
lore.culturalLegacy: Epimētheus survives in the language of hindsight. Every proverb about looking before leaping, every warning against opening Pandora's box, every discussion of unintended consequences rehearses his story. In cognitive science and economics, "epimethean" thinking names the backward glance that reorganizes judgment after the fact. The restoration Epimētheus keeps the Greek stress and length that mark him as the necessary twin of forethought.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Epimētheus is the god every human being meets in the small hours. He is the one who says, "If only I had known," the one who understands the warning only after the jar is open. His myth is not an invitation to despise him but to recognize him: we are all, at some moment, the afterthinker. The jar he opened cannot be closed, but Hope remains inside it — not as a remedy, but as the thing that makes the next opening possible.

To meditate on Epimētheus is to meditate on the irreversibility of choice. His name means afterthought, and afterthought is where wisdom is born, always too late for the mistake that fathered it. Yet without it there would be no learning, no regret, no change of mind. He is the patron of second thoughts, and second thoughts are the beginning of conscience.

lore.archaeology: Epimetheus is a purely textual figure: no sanctuary, cult image, or votive inscription names him. His witnesses are the manuscripts of Hesiod and Plato, the ceramic tradition that depicts Pandora and the jar, and the long afterlife of the myth in Western literature and philosophy.
